v.q: What does OpenID Connect (OIDC) add on top of OAuth 2.0?
o: An identity layer that tells the client who the user is
A faster way of refreshing access tokens
A new transport protocol for tokens
v.w: OAuth 2.0 answers what the app may access. OIDC answers who logged in, using an ID token and the userinfo endpoint.

v.q: Which statement about OIDC is NOT true?
v.w: OIDC is a thin identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0 and reuses its flows.

v.q: Which token carries the user's identity claims for the client app?
v.w: The ID token is a JWT meant for the client. The access token is meant for the API and should not be parsed by the client for identity.

v.q: Which token should a client use to learn who logged in?
v.w: The ID token is a JWT meant for the client and carries claims such as sub and email.

v.q: Which scope tells the server you want an OIDC login rather than plain OAuth?
v.w: Without `openid` the response is plain OAuth 2.0. `profile` and `email` request extra claims. `offline_access` requests a refresh token.

v.q: Which scope asks for the name and email of the user?
v.w: openid starts OIDC and the other scopes request claims about the user.

v.q: What is the `nonce` in an OIDC request for?
o: It ties the ID token to the request, so a captured token can't be replayed
It sets how long the user's session stays valid at the provider
It encrypts the ID token so only the client can read it
It picks which signature algorithm the provider will use
v.w: The client sends a random value and checks that the same value appears inside the ID token.

v.q: Which check does the nonce enable?
o: The ID token belongs to this login request
v.w: The client sends a random value and expects it back inside the signed ID token.

v.q: What must a client check in an ID token before trusting it?
o: Signature, issuer, audience (its own client id), expiry and nonce
Only that the string is a validly formed JWT token
Only that the same token has not been seen earlier today
Only that the user name inside the token is not empty
v.w: The `aud` must match the client, otherwise a token issued for another app could be replayed against yours.

v.q: Which check is NOT required for an ID token?
v.w: Validate signature, iss, aud, exp and nonce.

v.q: How does a client discover the endpoints and signing keys of an OIDC provider?
o: By hard-coding the values after reading them in a blog post
By scanning the open ports of the provider's servers
By asking each user to paste the endpoints in manually
v.w: The discovery document lists the issuer, authorization and token endpoints and `jwks_uri`, where the public keys rotate.

v.q: Where does a client find the endpoints and the signing keys of the provider?
v.w: Discovery lists the endpoints and the URL of the public keys, which rotate over time.

v.q: A resource server receives an ID token in the `Authorization` header instead of an access token. What is the right response?
o: Reject it, since ID tokens are for the client, not for APIs
Accept it, because it holds the user's name
Accept it only for read requests
Convert it into an access token first
v.w: Mixing up the two tokens is a common mistake. APIs should validate access tokens with the correct audience.

v.q: An API accepts an ID token as a bearer token. What is wrong with that?
o: It is meant for the client
v.w: The audience of an ID token is the client. APIs need an access token meant for them.

v.q: What does single sign-on (SSO) give users through OIDC?
o: One login at an identity provider that many apps trust
One password reused across all the apps
One shared cookie across every domain
v.w: Apps redirect to the identity provider. If the user already has a session there, they get back a token without typing credentials again.

v.q: Which statement about SSO with OIDC is NOT true?
o: Each app stores its own copy of the password
The identity provider authenticates the user
One login can serve many apps
v.w: Apps never see the password, which is the point of delegating to an identity provider.
